utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case number IT-01-47-T, Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution. Mr. Mundis, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Daryl Mundis, and our case manager, Ms. Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And could we have the appearances for the Defence, who aren't all present.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, and our legal assistant, Alexis Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and the other Defence team, who are all present.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to great everyone present, the members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else in the courtroom, as well as the interpreters who are outside the courtroom. We'll be hearing the witness scheduled for today now, and I would to ask the usher to bring the witness into the courtroom, please. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, while the usher is bringing the witness into the courtroom, I would just like to announce, Mr. President, that this is the only witness that we do have available for today, and I do not anticipate this requiring the full allotment of time that's scheduled for us. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day. I would first like to check that you're receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying. I will ask that question again. Are you receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying into English? No. It seems that we have a problem. And for the third time, I'll ask you whether you're receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying. If that is the case, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I read you very well now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called here as a witness for the Prosecution. You'll be testifying about events that happened in 1993. In order to do so, and before you take the solemn declaration, you should inform the Chamber of your first and last names and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Rolf Weckesser. The date of birth is the 12th of August of 1937.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could you tell me where you were born, which town or village, and which country you were born in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born at Freiburg which is in Germany, southern Germany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I can conclude that your nationality is German. Could you tell me what position you currently hold. What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm currently a pensioner. My former profession was an officer in the air force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What position did you hold, or what duties did you perform in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was assigned by the foreign ministry of Germany to the ECMM mission, and I was stationed at the time, from September until the end of December 1993 at Zenica, and I was a member of the RC Zenica, the Regional Centre Zenica, and under the RC Zenica, I was a member of the CC, coordination centre, Travnik. I was assigned there the function as a team leader, and the team was called V-4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you already testified before an international or national court with regard to the events that took place in 1993 in Bosnia and Herzegovina or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It's the second time I have to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember the case in which you testified, and were you a witness for the Prosecution or the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was witness for the Prosecution, and it was a case Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would now like to ask you to read out the solemn declaration that the usher will show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you have already given testimony, it won't be necessary for me to give you lengthy explanations of the procedure, as I have already said, you've been called here as a witness for the Prosecution. You have taken the solemn declaration, and that means that you should tell the truth and nothing but the truth. This means that you should not give false testimony. If a witness gives false testimony, he could be punished as a result. I wanted to point this important factor out. In addition, the provisions of this Tribunal state that if a witness, when responding to a question, thinks that his response could be used against him, he can refuse to reply to the question. In such a case, the Trial Chamber can compel the witness to reply, but the witness benefits from a form of immunity. You should provide clear and precise answers to the questions put to you. We'll be discussing things that took place over ten years ago, and your memory might not be accurate. If that is the case, please tell us. As this procedure is an oral procedure, which is sometimes supported by written documents, your oral testimony is the most important element in these proceedings. That is why your answers are that important. Once the Prosecution has concluded its examination-in-chief, Defence counsel, who are to your left, will also ask you questions in order to verify your credibility, as a witness or to obtain answers to questions that concern the political, military, or strategic context at the time. When the Defence has concluded its cross-examination, the Prosecution may re-examine you, and the three Judges sitting before you, in accordance with the Rules of the Tribunal, may ask you questions at any point in time in order to clarify certain answers or to fill in any gaps. As a rule, the Judges prefer waiting for the Prosecution and Defence to finish with their examination in order to ask the witness questions. The Judges' questions have only one -- questions in general have only one purpose, that is, to help in determining the truth. So roughly speaking, this is how we'll be proceeding, but this is no surprise to you, as you have already testified in a case. I will now let the Prosecution take the floor. I think Mr. Mundis will be conducting the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Weckesser. Can you please elaborate briefly upon your experience in the German air force with respect to what types of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. assignments or jobs you did while serving.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: I joined the German air force in 1957, and had the basic training as an officer. And then I had the ranks, standard ranks at all unit levels, at staff levels, to include international staff levels, all aiming into the main area, objective, of air defence. I was member of an international staff for a few years. I had also international positions as chairman of an international forum to do the operations of the Awacs aircraft and I had commander's functions. And my last function was commander of the German interception school at Erntebruck. I left the air force with the rank of a full colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, what was the date of your retirement from the German air force?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: The date of retirement was the end of March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, you told the Chamber that in 1993 you were working with ECMM. What was the date you commenced your assignment with ECMM?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: I commenced the assignment in May 1993, starting at the headquarters of the ECMM, at Zagreb, and taking first missions as a field observer south of Zagreb, in Croatia, then in the middle of Croatia, in the area of Pozega. Then I had an assignment in summer in Slavonski Brod, Eastern Slavonia. After that I had the assignment which is given reference here to the case, in Central Bosnia, from September until December. Then I took the function of a press advisor at the headquarters during the German Presidency. And after that, I finished mission in spring 1995 as the head of the coordination centre at Djakovo, which is Eastern Slavonia, close to Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. Weckesser, the period you were in Central Bosnia, you've told us September until December. What year was that?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: This was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You've told us that you were the team leader of V-4. Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber the structure of ECMM in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: The structure. I referred to the initial statement. We had a regional centre at Zenica, regional centres were set up all over former Yugoslavia to include neighbouring states, and below these regional centres, we had at Zenica three CCs, three coordination centres. I think it was Travnik, it was Mostar, and it was -- Travnik, Mostar -- oops. I'm leaving the last. Travnik, Mostar ... I'm missing one now at the moment. At least I belonged to the CC Travnik, and under the CC Travnik we had four field teams, V-1 through V-4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, what was the geographic area of V-4, the team that you led?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: The V-4 area was -- it was in the boundaries in the north, from Maglaj, Zavidovici, Zepce, at the northern point, aiming to the south, north of Zenica, excluding Zenica, going through the area of Kakanj, and then to the east up to Vares, into the north-east.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was your primary mission within this area that you've described for us?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: The objective, the mission, the primary mission, was, I think, threefold: To monitor, to assess, and to report the political situation was number one; to monitor, to assess, and to report the military situation was number two; and to monitor, assess, and report the humanitarian and the situation of the international rights was the third priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, how did you achieve these objectives? What did you do to achieve these objectives?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: We made all attempts just to gain ground, by talking with as many people as possible from the military, from the civilian arena, to the simple street people, in order to catch up feelings, developments, and directions, and in order to gain findings from all areas, from all levels. Basically, in my area, V-4, at that kind of field team, at the level of a field, it was a contributing factor to the higher levels, but basically it was aiming to the improvement of the conditions on the ground for the people, for instance, in order to arrange tripartite meetings which should finally lead then to some relaxation in regard to protection, in regard to water, electricity, or even to food. So it was my priority in that area at that time to open the area for free access in order to bring in food into the northern part, into the area of Maglaj and Zavidovici. These were enclaves surrounded, and they were really running into the danger to run out of food during the coming winter at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, can you tell the Trial Chamber what type of vehicles you used to monitor this area?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Our field work was -- for the field work, we used normally jeeps from different factories. Some were armed, some were armoured, and some were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what colour were these vehicles, and can you tell us any distinguishing features of these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: The cars were painted white, as we were wearing white clothes, as white as possible, to include helmet, and there was the EU sign painted on the cars. And we were wearing armbands, wearing the EU sign, and a certain blue hat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, you told us that part of your mission was to report. Can you tell the Trial Chamber how you reported the information that you obtained, including how frequently and at what times you reported this information?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: The timing of the reporting was every day the same, to include Saturday and Sunday. We moved out, depending on the intention for the respective day. Mostly very early, since we had, especially the team V-4, we had long travel distances to cover. Then we took our observations over the day, following a plan which was normally set up in the evening before. And mostly my team, we arrived as the last team. I mentioned the travel times that we had. So we arrived between normally 2000 and 2100 in the headquarters, in the Zenica hotel. We did our reporting. We normally did the report together, the two monitors were sitting together and were putting it into the computer. This report from the individual team, from the victor team, went then to the CC and it was there compiled in order to do a daily report of the CC.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how many people were in the team that you led?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: The team consisted of four persons. It was one leading, team leader, who decided actually about the aim of the day, and he also had the decision to do -- to decide if something was to be done or not to be done, to be continued or not to be continued, especially when the team was endangered. The second monitor, the deputy, was also full-time monitor, when we had a driver, and in addition changing interpreters going with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, at the time that you were in Central Bosnia, can you tell us who was the head of the regional centre, and also who was the head of the coordination centre?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: When I arrived, for a few days it was just a matter of transition. We had as the head of the RC, I think it was a French gentleman, Thebault, I think was his name, and Sir Martin Garrod arrived and he was until the end of my mission the head of the regional centre. The same on the side of the CC when I arrived for a very short time. It was a gentleman, a British gentleman, called Watkins, I think Philip Watkins, and he was replaced by a Canadian gentleman, Stutt Happ as the head of the CC.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, can you describe for us any type of training or briefings that you received either prior to your arrival in Central Bosnia or shortly thereafter?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: As a German monitor, I received a briefing at the foreign office before I left for the mission, at the headquarters, when arriving at Zagreb in May 1993, we got a very detailed briefing. It took almost one week, to include all aspects of the field work. At the RC Zenica, when arriving in September 1993 there, I got a very detailed briefing by the ops officer, Mr. Beaumont, a British monitor. And I had several Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. inbriefings, as I may call it, get-together with Sir Martin, exchanging views and also getting detailed findings which he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, Mr. Weckesser, the situation on the ground in Central Bosnia at the time when you arrived there in September 1993

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: The situation on the ground was, in my area -- should I specify on the area of V-4?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Was, at the beginning, calm. It seemed to be tense to a certain extent, as at that time the whole area was under tension. But in the eastern part, north-eastern part of Vares area, it seemed to be calm and nothing seemed to be moving. At least, it was not obvious to me. In the north, at Zepce, it was more active, and in Zavidovici there was a big tension. And therefore, we focused especially on this area, in order to break the ice between these partners. It was especially the Zepce Croatian-held enclave neighbouring the Bosnian-Muslim-held enclave of Zavidovici which were fighting each other, almost under the motherhood of surrounding Bosnian Serb forces. And it was the intention to break this kind of confrontation in order to at least get these two enclaves a possibility to peace, to settle down their fight, and in order to allow an entry of food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, during the period from September through December 1993, what military units were operating in the area patrolled and monitored by V-4?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: With the exception of the, as I may call it, HVO enclaves, Zepce and Vares, on the other side, it was all certain Bosnian corps-held territory, and I remember I had brigades in that area. It was the 303 Brigade, the 314 Brigade, and the 301 Brigade. But actually, I had mostly to do with the 303 Brigade, which was controlling the area which gave us access to the Zepce, Maglaj, Zavidovici pockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, you've told us about the situation being calm at the beginning of your tour. Can you describe for us whether or not that state changed over time.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: The situation started to change I think at the end of October, when we got surprisingly an information by the exiled government of Vares, which was stationed at that time in the area of Dabravine, that there were some atrocities taking place, done by HVO forces in a little village close to Vares called Stupni Do. This was around the 22nd, 23rd of October, and that was the time when really tension started in this area and was followed by quite a few actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Following this event in Stupni Do, you've told us quite a few actions followed. Can you please be a little more specific.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes. It led to the -- that my team and myself, we were trying to go to Stupni Do, following this cry for help. It was at the 24th, and we saw, from the main street, which is leading from Prozor up to Vares, we saw smoke over the hills coming out of the area where we expected Stupni Do to be located. But we did not get access. It was blocked by HVO forces in the town of Vares. It's the southern part of Vares. We were not allowed to go up there and to check what was happening there. At that date, I remember we met officers, BiH air force officers at the CP, and they were bitterly complaining that the UNPROFOR was not doing anything and was not helping. And they even set up an ultimatum saying if UNPROFOR is not doing anything, we will have to do something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, if I could briefly stop you for purposes of clarification. You mentioned the 24th. Can you please tell us the month and year that you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: It was the October in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you've also used the abbreviation "CP". Can you tell the Trial Chamber what CP meant.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: CP meant command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Weckesser, following these events in Stupni Do, what focus, if any, did you place on the community of Vares?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: The focus was primarily to find out about the fate of the inhabitants of Stupni Do and to try to rescue what was left. This was the prime focus during that time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time after that where you spent a period of time monitoring or patrolling Vares?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes. We did follow-up monitoring. We were continuously trying to get access to this little village. At the 25th, for instance, we went to -- we came together with HVO command people, the so-called Bobovac Brigade people, north of Vares, and we tried to ask for access from the commander there, and it was denied. So we again had no chance to get access to this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, I'd like to focus your attention on the first few days of November 1993. In the first few days of that month, were you in Vares at any time?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes. I remember we had one day, one other day, at Vares, at the 3rd November. At the 3rd November, we wanted again to monitor the situation at Vares. We entered the town early in the morning, and the streets were somewhat out of order. Two houses -- not two houses, but one apartment building in the main street was burning, and another one, neighbouring one, was also smoke coming out. We met about 30 Muslim inhabitants who were standing there lonely and lost in the marketplace. These were detainees. They had been detained before from the HVO in the elementary school. They were standing there, and I asked them if they would not try to extinguish the fires, and basically they agreed. We found one remaining Croatian fire brigade man who was still there. He was very eager to help, and he said the fire extinguishing gear is still available, so we could move out and we could fight the fire. We divided the group, by the help of another monitor who was coming on his transfer out from Tuzla. It was a man called Rudiger Lehmann. And we divided them into groups. Then they asked for cover, for protection, saying: Where are the PCs to protect us? Because there was still heard some single fire, small-arm fire, not close but far out. So they expected still having Croatian or HVO snipers, and since I could not provide any armoured cars in order to bring them to the fire scene, they said no, then they will not be helping us. And then we stopped this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, on the 3rd of November, 1993, when you were in Vares, did you see any members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: At the 3rd of November, I can't remember to have seen a single HVO man at that time, with one exception. We had -- it must have been in the afternoon, we had -- we went to the Franciscan monastery there and we were -- we were really almost attacked by two soldiers, HVO soldiers, trying to get out of town. They were obviously fleeing out and they tried to take the monks with them, and they also tried to take the car with -- our car. They were threatening us with weapons to give the car in order to get out. And finally, the monk convinced them to leave us alone and to leave them alone, and they cursed at us, but they went away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, when were you next in Vares after the 3rd of November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: It was already the next day, because when I reported at the evening to Sir Martin, to the head of the RC about the situation at Vares, he said he wanted to come with me so next day we went out again to Vares, and that was obviously the date or the time when 7th Muslim Brigade was moving into town, or had already moved into town. We went to the churchyard, to the monastery, in order to have a look for the fate of the monks there. At that place, when we got out of the car, it was very heavy small-arm firing into the tree on top of us. Leaves were falling down. On our feet there was lying on the ground a UN soldier, aiming with his rifle into nowhere. So we stood there for a few seconds, and Sir Martin was also looking into this area. There was no fight. It was actually just firing, because we didn't see any HVO soldiers at that time. So since we felt the situation to be very uncomfortable, we got into the car and we left the scene at that time. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, approximately what time on the 4th of November, 1993 did you arrive at the monastery?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: It must have been in the morning, around -- I assume it must have been 10.00, 10.00, 10.30, something like this, and I may add that we had before we left assured, through the UN soldier who was lying on the ground in front of the monastery door, that the three monks were safe in the cellar. After that, if I may add, we proceeded together then. We went out of Vares and we proceeded to the CP mentioned before at Dabravine, where Sir Martin and myself, we met another commander of the Bosnian forces, commander called Zubaca, who had a lengthy discussion with Sir Martin. Actually, I have no memory on this discussion, even if I was present. Maybe I had something to do, I had done something else, because on that discussion I have no memory left. After that, we went at the last step on that day to the monastery Kraljeva Sutjeska where Sir Martin took a chance to talk to the Guardian or the boss of the monastery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, you told us that on the 4th of November the 7th Muslim Brigade was moving into town. How do you know it was the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Nobody ever told me that this is the Muslim Brigade. I think this has happened I think to no monitor. But from the experience I had before, being in this area and looking to the forces I met almost daily, either in the area of Zepce/Zavidovici or in the area of Vares, there was a big change when Vares was retaken by the Bosnian forces. In the appearance of the military forces in this valley and at the town. Before the appearance of the military forces can be characterised by a kind of not-unique uniform. It seemed to be sometimes a little bit almost as an emergency clothing. The mood of the soldiers, as I remember, was, in general, not a very good one. There was fatigue. There was actually a lack of willingness to fight. And this had changed right before Vares was retaken by the Bosnian forces, and it was very -- it was obvious for us, especially in the area around the CP at Dabravine at that time, and at the entry of that valley, another one or two kilometres to the north, where the confrontation line itself was. Suddenly there were soldiers showing up who were eager, who were wearing clean uniforms, who were wearing uniforms which were suited to their body, not oversized or undersized, as we saw it before. And that led to the conclusion that we said we have a different forces, we have different forces, and another force. And the existence of the 7th Muslim Brigade as a spearhead was common knowledge among the monitors, and later on I think it was also underlined the assessment by my discussions which I had with the security officer Dugalic at Zenica of the 3rd Corps. He never commented, actually, when I said the 7th Muslim Brigade. I even tried to comment him -- to compliment him on the success of Vares, but he also never denied it, that the 7th Brigade was involved in the forces to take Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, after the 4th of November, 1993, when was the next time you went to the town of Vares?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: This was quite a while later, a few days later, because I had business at Zavidovici in order to prepare this humanitarian corridor. It was -- I think it was the 8th of November where we met the new town government at Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you told us earlier that you had met with the exiled government of Vares. Can you describe for us whether that was the same people that you subsequently met in Vares or if it was different people.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: No. It was, especially I remember the lady, a very dominant lady. She was the exile mayor. Her name was Mervana Hadzimurtezic. Very difficult to express for me. We met her twice, before she was taking charge again at Vares. She was very demanding, and asking us to help her to get back into her position at Vares. She was at all times saying she was trying to look for a multinational town, as it was before. She was always indicating that when she will come back into power, everyone will have the right to live there. And actually, after, at the 8th of November, we found her in place. She was telling us her -- telling us her -- as she was telling us this in advance. She had control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what, for the record, sir, it's a bit unclear, but what was her position when you met with her on the 8th of November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: She was the president of Vares, the town president.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what you observed when you departed Vares. First of all, tell us where you were going when you left Vares on the 8th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: It was, as I remember properly, if I remember properly, it was a strange picture at that time, because the streets were filled with people trying to loot, and even the roads leading towards Breza were covered with people carrying looted stuff to the south. This was the overall impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, who were these people that you saw carrying these goods?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: It was a mixture between soldiers and civilian people, and it was a strange mixture, and it was very surprising to me that after this retake of Vares and after these tensions which we had realised before and the uncertainty from the Bosnian forces to attack, and we felt that there was uncertainty about the future role of the Serbian forces, neighbouring, if they would support the Croatian forces, or the HVO forces. It was very strange that the army at that time could afford such a kind of out-of-order situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, you told us it was a mixture between soldiers and civilian people. My question is: How did you know some of these people were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: They looked, from the uniform, soldiers, some, and I even spotted -- I have clear in my mind, for instance, one soldier, which was just a grotesque situation, having on one shoulder the Kalashnikov, on the other one a vacuum cleaner, and just walking to the south, towards Breza.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weckesser.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no further questions in direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. And now on to the Defence. I'm giving the Defence counsel the floor for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Weckesser. We had a brief meeting yesterday. I would like to thank you for having given us an opportunity to talk to you before your testimony. Although I already introduced myself to you yesterday, I will do it again for the record. I'm Edina Residovic and I represent General Hadzihasanovic. Mr. Weckesser, the beginning of your tasks was in the Republic of Croatia and then, at the beginning of September, you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the beginning of September up to mid-December, according to your testimony, you were the leader of team V-4 in Central Bosnia and the area of your responsibility was between Vares, in the east, and Maglaj, in the west. Would that be correct? Or maybe north-west.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: North-west is a better description.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, would it be correct if I said that in the towns which were covered by your team, municipalities of Kakanj, Zepce, and Zavidovici belonged to the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, whereas the municipality of Vares at that time belonged to the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps and the municipality of Breza at that time belonged to the 6th Corps of the BiH army. Would this description reflect the situation in which your mission had its duties?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: With one exception. I could not accept your assessment that Vares was belonging to the 2nd Corps. I think this was an uncertainty, at least in my impression, between the two corps, who was really responsible for Vares. At that time, when the tensions were arising, because the reluctance to go for Vares from the 3rd Corps on one side, on the other side, the eagerness to drive to the north in order -- in addition to use the 7th Muslim Brigade for that, spoke for an area of interest of the 3rd Corps at Vares. And I think more than the 2nd Corps. We observed a very, very slow move from the 2nd Corps from Tuzla coming down in order to give some relaxation to the 3rd Corps in that critical situation where the uncertainty about the participation, of the possible participation of JNA forces were still pending. So with the exception of this comment, I think I accept your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since we have touched upon this issue, and you said that one of your main tasks was reporting on the military situation in the area, I am not going to talk about the specific events and the operation for the liberation of Vares. However, you can confirm that the municipalities of Kakanj and Vares are two neighbouring municipalities and that on the border between the two municipalities, there was a separation line between the two major corps of the BiH army, one whose headquarters was in Tuzla and the other whose headquarters was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. Missed where the headquarters of the other corps was.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: The headquarters of the 3rd Corps? No. 2nd Corps at Tuzla --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The 3rd in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has a document in front of him. Are there any objections on the part of the Defence for the witness's using this document that we don't know? First, the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. As far as I can see, the witness is holding a map in his hands. I don't know whether the Prosecution has discussed with the witness the utilisation of this map. Again, the Defence has the same objection as yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, certainly the witness was not instructed to rely upon a map or any other documents during the course of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Weckesser, you have understood the discussion. Because our procedure is oral, witnesses are not allowed to have any documents, unless the case is exceptional and when their memory has to be jogged a little. Usually in a different courtroom, we have a map. Unfortunately, today we are in a different courtroom and we cannot have that map at our disposal today. So as much as possible, avoid consulting the map. I'm turning to the Defence and I am giving them the floor to continue their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, I'd like to move on to another area now. We'll move on from geographical issues. In regard to the corps, we'd need a map to discuss this matter. In response to a question put to you by the Prosecution, you spoke about the main tasks and objectives of the European monitors. Nevertheless, could you confirm that when carrying out your mission, you had other tasks, for example, it was also your task to assist in humanitarian actions of other humanitarian organisations, it was your task to assist in establishing cease-fires. You were to assure liaison with the UNPROFOR headquarters and other international organisations. You were also to work on establishing trust between parties and to monitor and to report on the situation of the economy and of the infrastructure in your area. Were these additional tasks that you had?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: No. I think that is a full catalogue of the mission and the objectives in detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Vares. Could you tell me whether Vares was in an area that was of strategic importance for the 4th, 6th, the 1st, the 3rd, and the 2nd Corps of the BH army, and if that is the case, could you provide us with more explanations.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: You asked me as if I would be a military expert. If you ask me as a monitor at that time, to this aspect, yes, we thought -- it was a common understanding that Vares would have been a centre point, a real, vital point for the BH army, since it was the point where you actually could link all the corps in one piece, and especially if you could really support the Tuzla area on their own. So I agree that this was most likely a highly interesting strategic point.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that Vares is in a fairly difficult geographic area? This is a mountainous region, and there are mountain roads that go through this area, and these are not easy routes, even when the area is quite free; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: It's fully correct, and I can just underline it that the middle of my former V-4 area, the so-called mountain road which led from Kakanj through the mountains to the southern suburb of Zavidovici, this was our main concern that this little mountain road would not be usable in wintertime, in bad times, and support of the 40.000 inhabitants of Zavidovici could not be assured by this road. It was just an example for the statement, for the assessment you just made.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you have already said in response to a question put to you from the Prosecution, you said that before the BH operation to take over Vares, there was an HVO brigade in Vares. It was called the Bobovac Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we called them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that initially that brigade was attached to the 2nd Corps of the BH army, but at the end of September and in October, it refused to be under their command and was attached to the HVO in Kiseljak, or rather, to the Central Bosnia operations zone? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: I don't understand your question properly, because if you say would it be correct to say that initially that brigade was attached to the 2nd Corps of the BH army. There's a mistake in it. Because the Bobovac Brigade could not have been attached to the BH 2nd Corps. I think that's really a definite mistake in the question, isn't it? If you say -- I cannot comment on this if you ask me if the Bobovac Brigade, which was an HVO brigade, would have been initially attached to the 2nd Corps of the BH army. It cannot work like this. This would have been a big peace agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, you arrived there in September. I understand that. We won't pursue these questions any more. But just to clarify this, there were HVO brigades in Sarajevo too under the command of the 1st Corps, likewise in Tuzla, and they were under the command of the 2nd Corps. But since the question is not that important for our case, and I'm not a military expert either, we won't pursue the issue. You said that the legal authorities in Vares had fled, taken refuge in a village near Vares. Is it correct to say that those authorities had been expelled from Vares by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes. That is at least that what the exile mayor of Vares has told us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that at that time, the BH army was afraid about the open operation between the HVO and the Republika Srpska army, which had been in Travnik and Bugojno and in Zepce? This fear was very real in the area of Vares itself. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Can I answer your question only in part? I cannot comment on the situation in Travnik and Bugojno. I can comment on the situation in Zepce. There it was definitely real. I myself saw the Serbian tanks inside of Zepce. They tried to hide it, but I escaped once from my monitor, from the HVO side, and run into a Serbian tank platoon carrying the flag inside of Zepce. In Vares itself, I have not seen this participation. It was not materialised. But when I talked to officers of the BH army, they always gave me this indication that they were afraid about this kind of cooperation, or possible cooperation. On the other side, the HVO commanders from the Bobovac Brigade, they always were trying to convince us to relay the message to the Bosnian forces that they have still tanks and if they refer to tanks they refer to the Serbian tanks standing by, and it was obvious to give the message, to bring this message across that the BH forces should not attack Vares.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If Vares hadn't been liberated in the operation that you mentioned, and if the HVO and the Republika Srpska army had taken full control of Vares, would this have meant that the Tuzla area would have been completely cut off from all other areas under the control of the army?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: If you consider the mountains to the south-west of Tuzla as a real serious blockade of a reasonable connection, I would fully agree on this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When answering a question put to you by my learned colleague, you spoke about Stupni Do. If I have understood you correctly, HVO forces attacked Stupni Do. They completely destroyed the village and massacred the civilian population there. Are you personally aware of this?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Since I was the first ECMM member on scene there, yes, I was personally aware that a massacre had taken place. But I can't say that HVO forces have done the massacre. We have strong indications they have done it, but I have not seen them doing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you then find out that several hundred Bosniak civilians were imprisoned in a school in Vares?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes. It was right at the timing -- it was obviously at the time when this happened at Stupni Do that quite a number of males, of Muslim males, were arrested in the elementary school, and since we were afraid that they would be hurt and we had rumours that there were even being men killed, I went in Zenica to the ICRC and I convinced them to come on the scene with me, I think it was the next day, which was not so easy to get the ICRC involved. I had to declare these males as combatants before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke to HVO representatives, would it be correct to say that on that occasion you heard that this was in fact revenge for the crimes committed by the army in the Borovica and Kopjari villages, that after the Nordic Battalion entered and had been in Kopjari too, they determined that there were no traces of crimes there? Is what I have just told you correct, and does it correspond to the facts that you were familiar with at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: HVO representatives, after these tragic events, quite often were referring to these so-called massacres at Kopjari and Borovica. Personally, I also had a heated talk with -- after this happening, with the Guardian of the monastery at Vares, and he openly and plainly told me that, when I said, "Could you not avoid this thing in the suburb of your town," and this priest told me plainly they did the same in Kopjari.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, the investigation you carried out in Kopjari, as well as the investigation carried out by the Nordic Battalion in Borovica, didn't come up with any proof according to which crimes had been committed against the inhabitants of those villages; is that correct? And you reported on this in your daily reports?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: We also tried to get access to Borovica and Kopjari, the security officer of the 3rd Corps, Mr. Dugalic, denied the access. When the first rumour was spread about the suspected massacre, and he delayed me for two to three days, in order to get there. When we finally got there, we also had no indication for a massacre. The village itself was completely destroyed, but we saw no sign of massacre, and we did not realise any smell which was at that time unluckily familiar to me, of a massacre.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Father Stjepan Duvnjak. He is a father from an important religious institution, Kraljeva Sutjeska. Is it true to say that when speaking to Father Duvnjak, he would often tell you that the HVO was causing a lot of damage for the Croats in Central Bosnia because his propaganda made it necessary for them to leave the area where they were living and they went to live in Herzegovina as a result? Is that correct, and is this something that you included in your daily reports?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: I can't remember that that's what you are just asking was stated Father Stjepan Duvnjak, but exactly this statement was given to me by the -- not the mayor; by the priest of a Croatian town, Vukanovici, which is north of Kakanj, high in the mountains. He gave me exactly that statement, what you just referred to Stjepan Duvnjak. Actually, I can't remember that Stjepan Duvnjak told me this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I may have made a mistake as far as the name is concerned, because you mentioned Father Stjepan Duvnjak. Perhaps I've mixed up the names of the priest. I apologise. Are you aware of the fact that at the time, the HVO, by using propaganda, and in other ways, in fact tried to have the Croatian population move to parts which, according to the Vance-Owen Plan, in inverted commas, was supposed to belong to Croats? They did that in order to ensure a Croatian majority there, and as a result, this caused significant damage for the people in Central Bosnia. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: In general, I was aware of this. In specific, it was oriented to the case of Vukanovici. I think they were given hard pressure to get out, to move to Herceg-Bosna. And this village Vukanovici, guided by the priest, I think, they went out. In the meanwhile, their village was robbed by the neighbouring Muslim village, I think Zlokuca was the name. And when they were coming back, and it was just wintertime coming, they had nothing. They were living from the seeds, from -- given from UN, I think, in the spring before, and the seeds were spoiled by chemicals. So it was a very life-endangering situation for this village, and therefore, we did everything and tried everything and succeeded to get some food up to this lonely village. And I think it was interesting to see that the neighbouring -- the robbing as I saw it, I saw it at Zlokuca village, agreed to make a partnership with Vukanovici in order to protect them from robbing, from the robbery from other villages around. So I think it was a good partnership established, and Vukanovici, as I know, survived.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one more question in response to a question from the Prosecution. You said that on the 8th you were returning from Vares to Breza and you saw this strange column, composed of soldiers and civilians, and they were carrying items with them. Could you confirm that this trip from Vares to Breza, could you confirm that Breza at the time was in the zone of responsibility of the 6th Corps?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: No, I cannot. I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I've completed my cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It's almost time for the break. I think that the other Defence team will have some questions for the witness. Would it be best to have the break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think this is a good time for the break, and we can start with our cross-examination after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Weckesser, we'll have our so-called technical break now, and we will resume at about 5 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now resume, and the other Defence team will now conduct their cross-examination. They may take the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We only have a few questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Weckesser. On behalf of Mr. Kubura's Defence, I will just ask you a few questions in relation to your testimony today. On the 4th of November, you and Mr. Garrod were in Vares; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't notice anything unusual at the time, anything that was outside the framework of military operations in Vares?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: No, not as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You returned to Vares on the 8th of November; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You noticed the military units and some civilians looting certain property in Vares?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't recognise the units in question?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: If I told you that the brigade commander ordered that the entire unit of the 7th Brigade should leave Vares on the 5th of November, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: If that is correct, it would fit into my picture. If I may add, because I did not expect this picture from members of the 7th Brigade, since I had another picture before this happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: That means on the 8th of November, the 7th Brigade wasn't in Vares?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: It is an assumption on my side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, you met the representative of the civilian authorities, Mrs. Mervana Hadzimurtezic, and the commanding officer, Zubaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: As I stated before, I can't remember the meeting with this gentleman. But since it was stated in one of the records, and the records were always stating the reality, I'm sure I was within this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: If you assume that you were at the meeting, as you just said, the officer, Zubaca, wasn't an officer of the 7th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: This might be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have no further questions for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, I'll let you take the floor for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Weckesser, the soldiers that you saw leaving Vares on the 8th of November, did they appear to you to be withdrawing pursuant to any kind of military order?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: No, not at all. They seemed to be almost, in a way, as if they were working independent and almost dispersing from out of formation, military formation. It looked very unorganised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weckesser.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Weckesser, the Judges have some questions for you. First of all, I would like to be clear about your presence in Vares.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You have answered questions put to you by both parties. Nevertheless, there are certain things that aren't quite clear. Let's go back to the 3rd of November. You said that you arrived in Vares on the 3rd of November. When you arrived there on the 3rd of November, what was the situation in Vares? First of all, do you remember this? Because these events happened over ten years ago. Can you still recall with precision what you saw? Do you have a clear memory of what happened?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask, what kind of happenings you are referring now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the moment, the Trial Chamber isn't referring to any events. We are just referring to your arrival in Vares on the 3rd of November. When you arrived in Vares on the 3rd of November, what was the context within which you arrived in Vares on that day? Because you have told us that you arrived there on the 3rd of November. You then returned there. You asked Mr. Garrod to accompany you and you returned there on the 4th of November. So the Trial Chamber is interested in what you observed on the 3rd of November. What time did you arrive there, when, how, and what did you do on the 3rd of November, and at what time did you leave the town of Vares? If you can't remember, don't answer the question. But if you do remember the situation, please inform us of it. We don't want to cause any difficulties for you, but we would like to know what a witness who was present in the town on the 3rd of November was able to see.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: I'm just thinking about the sequence of events during this day. Sorry. I can't remember -- I can't answer the question in detail now, referring to the specific events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to refresh your memory. When answering the question put to you by the Prosecution, you said that on the 3rd of November there was disorder in the streets. You said there were detainees in the elementary school. You even found Croatian fireman there. Do you remember these events of the 3rd of November?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: I didn't know that you referred to these events. I already have detailed, Your Honours. Would you like me to repeat again in the way I saw it or I remember?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: As I remember, there was -- yes, there was disorder in the streets. UN soldiers were standing single, UN soldiers from the NordBat Battalion were standing in the marketplace, actually, I had the feeling, not knowing what they were protecting. We approached this elementary school, where we assumed that the arrested Muslims were kept, and I stepped forward and talked to the HVO soldier who was very unfriendly to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In what language did you speak? English?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the HVO soldier spoke English, he understood you when you spoke English?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: No. It was transferred by the translator. And it obviously went --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: It was by translator. An interpreter we had with us, and it was obviously leading in a heated discussion to a point where the interpreter told me: "We should better go. He's getting really serious now." And I remember about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this stage, was it confirmed to you that there were Muslim detainees in the elementary school and that these detainees were detained by the HVO? Was that confirmed to you by that stage?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: I did not see the detainees because they didn't let me enter, because they didn't let me pass through the entrance. Three soldiers were standing there in front of it and I was standing below and asking for access, and they denied it. And about five metres to the right, out of a bush, there were soldiers aiming to us with a gun, you know, the interpreter warned me and said we should better go now. Because we had a heated debate and I tried to force him to let me in and to have a look, but it did not work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you left Vares at what time, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: I can't remember in detail. It must have been afternoon time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 3rd November, you saw soldiers of the HVO. In the streets, did you also see civilians who were there, or were they just HVO soldiers? Do you remember having seen anybody else but the troops in the streets?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: I cannot remember having seen anybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on to the 4th of November. You went back to Vares with Mr. Garrod; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: It is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You arrived in Vares at what time, approximately, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: It must have been between 10.00 and 11.00, looking to the travel time, it took us normally -- we departed normally at 7.30, 8.00, and it took us one and a half hour, about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you arrived in the town, did you have to pass through any checkpoints or did you just drive in your car straight to the town without stopping and having any problems?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: I can't remember having been stopped by a checkpoint at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You arrived, you went to the centre of town. Where did you arrive? Where did you find yourself? At what point in the town?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: We right away went to the centre of the town, which is the church, and also the housing of the monks, just associated to the church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that place, were the buildings destroyed? Were they set on fire? Were there any civilians in the streets? Were there any troops in the streets? What did it look like to you?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: I saw no buildings being destroyed. I saw smoke, but I don't think that it was smoke coming from houses. It was just smoke from the firing. I saw no civilian at that time, not a single one, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You arrived during the period of tensions, and there was a conflict. Was there still shooting going on or had that stopped by the time you arrived?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: It was a very strange situation. Initially we saw there's a fight going on, or I saw there's a fighting going on, looking to these big small-arms fires, but I realised there was no enemy, there was no fighting against an enemy. It was a kind of celebration of victory, and it almost seemed as a big celebration of a victory, maybe an unexpected victory like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there was celebratory shooting. Those who celebrated, did you see them? Were they soldiers? Did they wear uniforms? Did they have any insignia? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: I saw soldiers. I did not recognise insignia. I did not look to the soldiers in detail, because I was really busy about our protection, since we were afraid to get shot at by occasion, since we were actually in the middle of a shooting into the trees right above us. And it looked very strange, which led to the conclusion that we should better leave this place. And it was also interesting to see that the UN soldiers were lying flat on the ground and trying to protect himself from unintentional shooting on him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the UN soldiers were on the ground, trying to protect themselves. You were in a white uniform, and the soldiers who were celebrating their victory were shooting all the time. These soldiers who were shooting, although it was a long time ago, they wore uniforms. What kind of uniforms did they wear? Camouflage uniforms? Did they wear military uniforms, or did they look like infantry soldiers? You had a quick glance. I know that it was a long time ago, but this was an unusual situation for a town like that. So what do you remember about these men who were shooting? What did they look like?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: It was at that time not my full concentration on the outfit. I can't remember in detail, not in any aspect you just mentioned, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have told us that you returned on the 8th of November. When you returned four days later, you had information that the situation had calmed down, otherwise you would not have returned. What were the motives that compelled you to go back to that town on the 8th of November? Were there any new conditions in place that made you return after four days?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: There was not a special intention on this. It belonged to our normal tasking to monitor continuously, as much as possible. We would have gone even if the fighting would have still -- having been going on and trying to get access to the situation. After the break, and I had nothing different, other duties the days before, it was just time again to look how the situation has settled, what are the changes, how are the political situations, what kind of government is now in chain and what is the situation of the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. You saw the situation there. Did you formulate that? Did you write that the authorities were municipal authorities headed by Mrs. Hadzimurtezic? Did you report to UNPROFOR or the military authorities after having seen all that? What did you do? Did you do anything, having inspected the situation there?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: We, myself, I reported that I found the -- Mrs. Mervana Hadzimurtezic in place, governing the town, being in deep sorrow about feeding the population and asking at that time, in a very demanding way, for access to warehouses, which were blocked by, as I remember French legion forces which have come over from Sarajevo to help out the NordBat. And as I remember, there was a gentleman in that meeting from Sarajevo. He introduced himself as a minister. And he also was demanding the access to give free the warehouse access. At that meeting was also present, as I remember, Colonel Henriksson from the NordBat, the commander, and actually, the pressure was from him to withdrew the troops because he was the military representative. And as I remember, they made an ultimatum saying either you give up the blockade of the warehouses or we will use military pressure. And as I remember, Colonel Henriksson found a way by asking for an ultimatum in order to ask for -- to gain -- asked for some time to do the preparation to give up that blockade in order to avoid the stressing ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This depot, according to you, there was a blockade, and those who were guarding the depot were the NordBat troops; am I right? And in the municipality of Vares, you had access, and you asked them to lift the blockade, and I believe that I understood that it took some time, and the NordBat was reluctant to do that. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe I have displayed it in the wrong way. The depots -- I don't know. I can't remember what the depots were, was this property of UN or was this property of the town itself. And as I said, astonishing to me, the French Foreign Legion forces, they took immediately when they came in, they obviously saw a task for them, to guard the warehouses from looting, and they just blocked access for everybody, to include the possible new owner of this warehouses, which were also the town government now. So the government -- town government just claimed her right to say, "I would like to have access to my warehouses. And now you have forces there." And by asking this, it was assumed by the town government that the NordBat is a superior military organisation running the area, and the foreign legion company or squadron is just only an add-on, and subordinate unit in that case, a helping unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this depot was guarded by the French Foreign Legion troops. And finally, the municipality could gain access to the depot, after a while?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't remember, do you. Very well, then. My last question, which does not concern the town of Vares. To a question put to you by the Defence, you answered about the importance of Vares with regard to the routes leading to Vares and the supplies that could be brought to that town. You're a soldier who served in the air force. Looking back at that area, what about the air lift? Was that possible for the supply of humanitarian aid and food? Was an air lift a possibility? Was that never envisaged for this particular location that was not so easy to access?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: That's a very difficult question, Your Honours. I think the UNHCR didn't have the means to do an air lift in that -- or to envisage such an air lift in that dimension because Tuzla is a big area and they were really close to getting short of food. And as an example how necessary this route actually was for the BiH was a convoy which we succeeded to get through this area for Tuzla, just one or two weeks before, it was a convoy of joy, it was called. And it started, I think, in Split, with around 100 trucks, and finally by taking away from all the transit partners which had been passed, different warring parties, I think only 50 trucks were coming to Tuzla. But it was keenly needed in Tuzla at that time. And this route through Vares was used at that time, and at that time it seemed to me the only way to give help to this area, or at least to get some help through to this area. If there were plans for aerial support from the UNHCR, I don't know, but I cannot imagine, because I think the means were not available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the military means is concerned, was it possible to engage planes to deliver medical aid or other supplies? Would that have been possible or not, as an option?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Definitely it could have been an option, if the UN would have been willing to do it, or another helping organisation. It would also have been a possibility to include air drops or such things, which -- how they have been done later on in Maglaj and in the other pockets. But actually it was not part of our mission. It was not part of our planning. It was not part of our thinking. We were concentrating on the things on the ground, not in the air.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm going to ask my colleagues whether they have any questions to put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Just two small questions, Colonel, on what you saw on the 11th of November, when you returned to Vares. You saw looting, you saw people carrying goods to the south, and you saw that these people were civilians, as well as military. When asked by the Defence, you said: I don't think these were people from the 7th Brigade because I didn't expect these things from that brigade. And earlier in the morning, you said: On the 4th of November, I could distinguish the 7th Brigade from other soldiers on the basis of the very different appearance. They were better -- had better clothes, more spirit, and were more motivated than other soldiers I used to meet. Based on that description, on the difference you apparently noticed between members of that brigade and other soldiers, could you go back to the 11th of November and tell me, if possible, to what category of soldiers those soldiers belonged that you saw on the 8th of November.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. You initially said -- you are talking about the 11th, but you mean the 8th of November? You said first the 11th of November, but it's the 8th. I have also the problem with the sequence of the dates. As I said, the behaviour was so much different that I could not assume that this is any more the 7th Brigade. This was the formation, the appearance which did not fit into the appearance of the formation which was already to take Vares again, you know, just before it was taken. This was very, very different. So I can assume, and I must assume, that there has been a change of personnel or a withdrawal of this spearheading 7th Brigade. It did not fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So if I may resume what you said just before, they didn't like -- they didn't appear to be soldiers of the 7th Brigade. Is that a summary of what you said?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. The second question on the 11th is very simple. When you observed people looting and carrying goods away to the south, did you see any attempts to stop them?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Not at all. Not at all. I remember I saw the doors of the houses open, people coming out, moving out, and then undisturbed a long string of people moving out of town. So everyone was actually taking care of his intentions on his own, so he was -- there was nobody trying to stop it or to get it organised or whatever. It seemed to be very organised, a kind of free movement of everyone trying to get what he could get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: What made you think that this was well organised, then?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Not organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Not organised? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Nothing organised. It seemed to me as a matter of occasion, as taking the chance now. It did not look -- not at all organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Was there any military presence that would have been able to prevent this at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: There was military presence possible, but it would have been an intervention which would not have been very wise after this tense area before, tense time before, and the warehouse issue and all these things. The NordBat Battalion could have done something, but if I would have been the commander at that time, I would not have intervened in that kind of undertaking of the population and of the people, because this was not warring, there was nobody hurt at that time. There were, I think, more difficult things now to look, that refugees and remaining Croatian people had to be protected properly. This had more importance. And I remember -- I can't exactly remember if it was that day when we were going out, we were stopped by -- this was before, far before, during the transition of the power, when the HVO was withdrawing. We were stopped by Muslim ladies in front of a building in the entrance of Vares, and they were trying -- "There are soldiers from the HVO harassing us." And so we immediately went to the NordBat and I asked Colonel Henriksson to look for these women in that apartment building, and he immediately sent some soldiers with PCs down there in order to take care. I think these were other priorities in the environment of that situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: My question was not to ask you whether NordBat or any other international presence should have prevented or could have prevented that, but it was more directed to the presence of the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: ROLF WECKESSER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. That is for me almost impossible to assess. If I give you my impression, I think they were all busy to do this kind of business at that time. There was very limited military reorganisation of the whole environment. There was a kind of chaotic situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges have asked certain questions that may have revealed new elements arising from these questions. Will the Prosecution have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, the Prosecution's position is that the party calling the witness should be the last one to put any questions. Our view would be that the Defence, if they have questions, should put those questions prior to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. General Hadzihasanovic's Defence does not have any additional questions to put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, after the Judges' questions, we do not wish to put any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence doesn't have any questions. Mr. Mundis, do you have any?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, we don't, Mr. President. The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Colonel, your testimony has come to an end. We would like to thank you for having come to The Hague to testify, to have enabled us to learn certain things about the events that took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1993, especially during the period when you were a member of the European Monitoring Mission. Once again, we would like to thank you. We wish you a happy journey back home. I'm going to ask Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
